title: Gravitation and Cosmology
text:
Preface
These are my notes from the course Gravitation and Cosmology. They are based on S. Weinberg, Gravitation and Cosmology: Principles and Applications of the General Theory of Relativity (Wiley, 1972), with the black holes of Lecture 15 following S. M. Carroll, Spacetime and Geometry (Addison-Wesley, 2004). The course builds general relativity from the principle of relativity and the equivalence principle, derives the Einstein equations, and applies them to the tests in the solar system, black holes, gravitational waves and the expansion of the Universe.

title: 1  The Principle of Relativity and the Equivalence Principle
text:
The principle of relativity
The aim of the course is to formulate general relativity as a theory of gravity, and to use it to describe
This lecture introduces the principle of relativity and the equivalence principle, and shows how the two together lead to general relativity.
The content of the principle lies in which coordinate systems count as admissible. We go through Newtonian mechanics, special relativity and general relativity in turn.
crumbs: 1  The Principle of Relativity and the Equivalence Principle

title: 1  The Principle of Relativity and the Equivalence Principle
text:
NoteDefinition 1.1 (Principle of relativity). [1, Ch. 1]



The principle of relativity states that the equations expressing the laws of physics have the same form in all admissible coordinate systems. A theory that obeys it is a theory of relativity.




Newtonian mechanics






NoteDefinition 1.2 (Reference frames).



A reference frame is a three-dimensional spatial coordinate system with a clock at every point. It is inertial if every free particle moves along a straight line at constant speed.


In Newtonian mechanics the admissible coordinate systems are the inertial ones, at rest or in uniform motion with respect to absolute space. Two of them, \((t, \vec x)\) and \((t', \vec x')\), are related by a Galilean transformation \[\vec x' = R\vec x + \vec v t + \vec d, \qquad t' = t + \tau, \tag{1}\] with \(R\) a rotation, \(\vec v\) a constant velocity and \(\vec d\), \(\tau\) constant translations. These form the 10-parameter Galileo group: three angles for \(R\), three components each for \(\vec v\) and \(\vec d\), and one for \(\tau\) [1, Ch. 1].






CautionExample 1.3 (A free particle).



The equation of motion of a free particle of mass \(m\) is \[m\,\frac{d^2\vec x}{dt^2} = 0, \tag{2}\] a straight line in the \((t, \vec x)\)-plane. Inverting (1) gives \(\vec x = R^{-1}(\vec x' - \vec v t - \vec d)\) and \(t = t' - \tau\), so (2) becomes \(m R^{-1}\, d^2\vec x'/dt'^2 = 0\). Since \(R\) is invertible, \(m\, d^2\vec x'/dt'^2 = 0\): the equation has the same form in every inertial frame.


There are two ways an equation can keep its form. Take rotations only (\(\vec v = \vec d = 0\)).






NoteDefinition 1.4 (Invariance and covariance).



A quantity is invariant if it does not change under a transformation. If \(S\) and \(P\) are scalars, \(S' = S\) and \(P' = P\), then \(S = P\) implies \(S' = P'\), and the equation is invariant.
An equation is covariant if both sides transform in the same way. If \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\) are vectors, \(\vec a' = R\vec a\) and \(\vec b' = R\vec b\), then \(\vec a = \vec b\) becomes \(R^{-1}(\vec a' - \vec b') = 0\), and since \(R\) is invertible, \(\vec a' = \vec b'\).


Newtonian mechanics is covariant under Galilean transformations by construction.






TipRemark 1.5 (The end of Galilean invariance).



Maxwell’s equations are not Galilean invariant: under a Galilean boost the speed of light would change. In the 19th century this was explained by an ether filling space, relative to which light has a fixed speed. The Michelson–Morley experiment looked for the resulting difference in the speed of light along perpendicular directions and found none.




Special relativity
Special relativity rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and the speed of light is the same for all observers. The admissible coordinate systems are still the inertial ones, but they are now related by Lorentz transformations rather than Galilean ones.






NoteDefinition 1.6 (Poincaré transformation). [1, Ch. 2]



A Poincaré (or inhomogeneous Lorentz) transformation is a map \[\xi^\alpha \mapsto \xi'^\alpha = \Lambda^\alpha{}_\beta\, \xi^\beta + a^\alpha, \qquad \Lambda^\alpha{}_\gamma\, \Lambda^\beta{}_\delta\, \eta_{\alpha\beta} = \eta_{\gamma\delta}, \tag{3}\] where \(\xi^\alpha = (t, \vec x)\), \(\eta_{\alpha\beta} = \operatorname{diag}(-1, 1, 1, 1)\) and \(a^\alpha\) is constant. When \(a^\alpha = 0\) it is a Lorentz transformation. The condition on \(\Lambda\) says that the Minkowski metric \(\eta_{\alpha\beta}\) is invariant.


The Poincaré transformations are the most general maps between inertial frames: rotations, boosts and spacetime translations. They form the full symmetry group of special relativity.






CautionExample 1.7 (A free particle in special relativity).



The equation of motion of a free particle is \[\frac{d^2\xi^\alpha}{d\tau^2} = 0, \qquad d\tau^2 = -\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, d\xi^\alpha d\xi^\beta, \tag{4}\] with \(\tau\) the proper time. For \(\alpha = 0\) this gives \(dt/d\tau = \text{const}\), and the motion is again a straight line in the \((t, \vec x)\)-plane.
Under (3), \(d\xi'^\alpha = \Lambda^\alpha{}_\beta\, d\xi^\beta\), so \[d\tau'^2 = -\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, \Lambda^\alpha{}_\gamma \Lambda^\beta{}_\delta\, d\xi^\gamma d\xi^\delta = -\eta_{\gamma\delta}\, d\xi^\gamma d\xi^\delta = d\tau^2.\] Proper time is invariant, and therefore \[\frac{d^2\xi'^\alpha}{d\tau'^2} = \Lambda^\alpha{}_\beta\, \frac{d^2\xi^\beta}{d\tau^2} = 0.\]




General relativity
In general relativity all coordinate systems \(x^\mu = (t, \vec x)\) are admissible. The transformations between them, \[x^\mu \mapsto x'^\mu(x), \tag{5}\] are arbitrary smooth invertible maps, called general coordinate transformations or diffeomorphisms. The resulting covariance is called general covariance or diffeomorphism covariance; it is discussed in Lecture 8.

title: 1  The Principle of Relativity and the Equivalence Principle
text:
The equivalence principle
An inertial force acts on every mass in a non-inertial frame. By Newton’s second law every inertial force is proportional to the mass it acts on. So is gravity, and this led Einstein to ask whether gravity is itself an inertial force. An observer in a closed box in free fall cannot detect the gravitational field: a freely falling frame behaves like an inertial one (Figure 1.1).






Figure 1.1: Left: in a box at rest on the Earth, a released ball falls to the floor. Right: in a freely falling box, the ball floats as it would in empty space. Locally, gravity can be transformed away.



To see how inertial forces arise, apply a general transformation (5) to \(m\, d^2x^i/dt^2 = 0\), with \(t' = t'(t, \vec x)\) and \(x'^i = x'^i(t, \vec x)\). By the chain rule, \[\frac{d^2 x^i}{dt^2} = \frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial t'}\frac{dt'}{dt} + \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^j}\frac{dx'^j}{dt}\Bigr),\] and solving for \(d^2x'^i/dt'^2\) leaves terms on the right-hand side. These terms, multiplied by \(m\), are the inertial forces.






CautionExample 1.8 (A rotating frame).



Let \((t, \vec x)\) be inertial and let \((t', \vec x')\) rotate counter-clockwise about the \(z\)-axis with constant angular velocity \(\omega\): \[t' = t, \quad x' = x\cos\omega t + y\sin\omega t, \quad y' = -x\sin\omega t + y\cos\omega t, \quad z' = z.\] A free particle then obeys \[m\,\frac{d^2\vec x'}{dt'^2} = -2m\, \vec\omega \times \frac{d\vec x'}{dt'} - m\, \vec\omega \times (\vec\omega \times \vec x'),\] the Coriolis and centrifugal forces.








CautionExample 1.9 (A uniformly accelerated frame).



Let \(t' = t\) and \(\vec x' = \vec x - \tfrac12 \vec a\, t^2\), a frame accelerating in the direction of \(\vec a\). A free particle then obeys \[m\,\frac{d^2\vec x'}{dt'^2} = -m\,\vec a.\] With \(\vec a = (GM/R^2)\, \hat{\vec r}\) this inertial force coincides with the gravitational force of a mass \(M\) at distance \(R\).


Should gravity therefore be thought of as an inertial force? A priori there is no reason for the inertial mass \(m\), which measures the resistance to acceleration, to equal the gravitational mass \(m_g\), which measures the strength of the coupling to a gravitational field.
Let \((t, \vec x)\) be inertial and let a test particle move in a gravitational field \(\vec g(t, \vec x)\): \[m\, \frac{d^2\vec x}{dt^2} = m_g\, \vec g(t, \vec x).\] Pass to the freely falling frame \(t' = t\), \(\vec x' = \vec x - \tfrac12 \vec g\, t^2\). Then \[m\,\frac{d^2\vec x'}{dt'^2} = (m_g - m)\,\vec g - 2m t\, \frac{d\vec g}{dt} - \tfrac12 m t^2\, \frac{d^2\vec g}{dt^2}.\] If \(m_g = m\), the field cancels up to terms in the derivatives of \(\vec g\). Gravity cannot be removed everywhere when the field is inhomogeneous or time-dependent, but in a small enough neighbourhood these derivative terms are negligible. Locally, gravity is an inertial force.






NoteDefinition 1.10 (Equivalence principle). [1, Ch. 3]



The weak equivalence principle is the statement \(m_g = m\).
The strong equivalence principle states that at every spacetime point \(X\) there is a coordinate system \(\xi^\alpha_X\) such that, in a sufficiently small neighbourhood of \(X\), the laws of physics take the form they have in special relativity in the absence of gravity. Such a \(\xi^\alpha_X\) is called a locally inertial or freely falling coordinate system.


General relativity is then a framework for particle mechanics and electrodynamics whose equations

are covariant under general coordinate transformations (the principle of relativity), and
reduce to those of special relativity in a locally inertial coordinate system (the equivalence principle).

title: 1  The Principle of Relativity and the Equivalence Principle
section: Free fall in a gravitational field
text:
Free fall in a gravitational field
Consider a particle that moves under gravity alone. In a locally inertial coordinate system \(\xi^\alpha\) it is free, and by (4) \[\frac{d^2\xi^\alpha}{d\tau^2} = 0, \qquad d\tau^2 = -\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, d\xi^\alpha d\xi^\beta.\] Now pass to an arbitrary coordinate system \(x^\mu\), in which the effects of gravity appear, with inverse \(\xi^\alpha(x)\). Then \[0 = \frac{d}{d\tau}\Bigl(\frac{\partial\xi^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu}\frac{dx^\mu}{d\tau}\Bigr) = \frac{\partial\xi^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu}\frac{d^2x^\mu}{d\tau^2} + \frac{\partial^2\xi^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu \partial x^\nu}\frac{dx^\mu}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\nu}{d\tau}.\] Multiplying by \(\partial x^\lambda/\partial\xi^\alpha\) and using \(\frac{\partial\xi^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu}\frac{\partial x^\lambda}{\partial\xi^\alpha} = \delta^\lambda_\mu\) gives the following.






NoteDefinition 1.11 (Affine connection and metric tensor). [1, Ch. 3]



The affine connection and the metric tensor are \[\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} = \frac{\partial x^\lambda}{\partial\xi^\alpha}\frac{\partial^2\xi^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu \partial x^\nu}, \qquad g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\alpha\beta}\, \frac{\partial\xi^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu}\frac{\partial\xi^\beta}{\partial x^\nu}.\]








ImportantProposition 1.12 (Equation of motion in free fall). [1, Ch. 3]



A particle moving under gravity alone satisfies \[\frac{d^2x^\lambda}{d\tau^2} = -\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\, \frac{dx^\mu}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\nu}{d\tau}, \qquad d\tau^2 = -g_{\mu\nu}\, dx^\mu dx^\nu. \tag{6}\]


Equation (6) cannot be solved until we know how \(g_{\mu\nu}\) and \(\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\) depend on the spacetime point. Formulating general relativity as a theory of gravity thus has two parts:

express all effects of gravity on particles and electromagnetic fields in terms of \(g_{\mu\nu}\) and \(\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\);
find a dynamical equation for the metric, which also determines the affine connection.







TipRemark 1.13 (The Newtonian analogy).



In Newtonian gravity a particle obeys \(d^2\vec x/dt^2 = -\nabla\phi\), which cannot be solved without knowing the potential \(\phi\). The potential is fixed by the mass density \(\rho\) through the Poisson equation \(\nabla^2\phi = 4\pi G\rho\). In general relativity the metric plays the role of the potential, and the Einstein equations (Lecture 11) play the role of the Poisson equation: given the distribution of energy and momentum, they determine the metric, and with it the motion of particles.

title: 1  The Principle of Relativity and the Equivalence Principle
text:
Gravity as geometry
The equivalence principle suggests a change of perspective, which the following example makes concrete.






CautionExample 1.14 (An apple falling from a tree).



In the Newtonian picture, the Earth produces a gravitational field that accelerates the apple towards the ground. In general relativity the apple is in free fall: by Proposition 1.12 it moves on a geodesic, and its worldline is as “straight” as a worldline can be. It is the observer standing on the ground who is accelerated, pushed upwards by the ground, and from their point of view the apple appears to fall (Figure 1.2). Light needs no separate treatment: it also moves on geodesics, so to the observer on the ground it too appears to bend.








Figure 1.2: Worldlines of the Earth’s surface, an observer on it and an apple. Left: the Newtonian picture, in which the apple accelerates. Right: the free-fall picture, in which the apple moves on a straight line and the surface accelerates. (Schematic: a flat diagram cannot show curvature.)



The second picture also explains why inertial and gravitational mass are equal: the observed acceleration does not depend on the falling object at all, just as for the inertial forces of Examples 1.8 and 1.9.






TipRemark 1.15 (Spacetime becomes dynamical).



In Newtonian mechanics and in special relativity, space and time form a fixed background: the arena in which particles and fields move, but which is not itself affected by them. In general relativity, space and time are combined into spacetime, a manifold with a metric \(g_{\mu\nu}\), and the metric is a dynamical field in its own right. It tells matter how to move, through the geodesic equation (6), and is in turn determined by the distribution of energy and momentum, through the Einstein equations \[R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12\, g_{\mu\nu} R = -8\pi G\, T_{\mu\nu}\] of Lecture 11. Gravity is then not a force acting in spacetime, but the curvature of spacetime itself. Even without any matter, the metric has degrees of freedom of its own: gravitational waves (Lecture 16) are ripples of spacetime that propagate through empty space.

title: 2  Special Relativity and Lorentz Transformations
text:
Lorentz transformations
Special relativity is a framework for particle mechanics and electrodynamics whose equations
The second requirement plays the same role here as the equivalence principle does in general relativity (Definition 1.10).
Let \(x^\alpha\) and \(x'^\alpha\) be the coordinates of two inertial coordinate systems. They are related by a Poincaré transformation (Definition 1.6) \[x'^\alpha = \Lambda^\alpha{}_\beta\, x^\beta + a^\alpha, \qquad \Lambda^\alpha{}_\gamma\, \Lambda^\beta{}_\delta\, \eta_{\alpha\beta} = \eta_{\gamma\delta}.\] The condition on \(\Lambda\) is exactly what is needed to leave the proper time invariant, \[d\tau^2 = -\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, dx^\alpha dx^\beta = dt^2 - |d\vec x|^2.\]
The surfaces \(d\tau^2 = 0\) through a point form its light cone (Figure 2.1). A Lorentz transformation preserves it, and so preserves the split into timelike (\(d\tau^2 > 0\)), lightlike (\(d\tau^2 = 0\)) and spacelike (\(d\tau^2 < 0\)) separations.
Conversely, the Lorentz transformations are the only non-singular linear transformations that preserve \(d\tau^2 = 0\) for every light signal and fix the scale of \(d\tau^2\). This makes them the physically relevant class of transformations between inertial frames.

title: 2  Special Relativity and Lorentz Transformations
text:
ImportantProposition 2.1 (The speed of light is frame independent). [1, Ch. 2]



A signal that moves at the speed of light in one inertial frame moves at the speed of light in every inertial frame related to it by a Lorentz transformation.






NoteProof





Along the path of the signal, \[d\tau^2 = dt^2\bigl(1 - |d\vec x/dt|^2\bigr) = 0.\] Since \(d\tau'^2 = d\tau^2\), \[0 = d\tau'^2 = dt'^2\bigl(1 - |d\vec x'/dt'|^2\bigr),\] so \(|d\vec x'/dt'| = 1\). \(\square\)











CautionExample 2.2 (A plane wave).



Consider the monochromatic plane wave \(e^{i(|\vec k|t - \vec k\cdot\vec x)}\). Its wave fronts move so that the phase is constant, \[\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(|\vec k|\, t - \vec k\cdot\vec x\bigr) = 0,\] which is solved by \(d\vec x/dt = \vec k/|\vec k|\), a speed of one. Along the wave front \(d\tau^2 = 0\), so by Proposition 2.1 it moves at the speed of light in every inertial frame.









Figure 2.1: The light cone at a point. Timelike worldlines stay inside it and light rays run along it; Lorentz transformations map the cone to itself.

title: 2  Special Relativity and Lorentz Transformations
text:
Some differential geometry
Let \(\mathcal M\) be a smooth manifold with tangent space \(T_p\mathcal M\) at each point \(p\).






NoteDefinition 2.3 (Tangent bundle).



The tangent bundle of \(\mathcal M\) is the disjoint union of all its tangent spaces, \[T\mathcal M = \bigsqcup_{p \in \mathcal M} T_p\mathcal M.\]


On a curved manifold, vectors at different points live in different tangent spaces, with different bases, so they cannot be added or subtracted directly. In particular, the derivative of a vector field along a curve is not defined without extra structure.






NoteDefinition 2.4 (Affine connection, informally).



An affine connection on \(\mathcal M\) is a rule that connects nearby tangent spaces. It says how to transport a vector along a curve “without changing its direction”, which makes the manifold look infinitesimally like Euclidean space and allows vector fields to be differentiated.


The connection coefficients \(\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\) of Definition 1.11 are the components of such a connection. The precise definition, through the covariant derivative, comes in Lecture 7.

title: 3  Lorentz Transformations and Tensors
text:
The Lorentz group
Consider a homogeneous Lorentz transformation \(x'^\alpha = \Lambda^\alpha{}_\beta\, x^\beta\), so that \[\eta_{\alpha\beta} = \Lambda^\gamma{}_\alpha\, \Lambda^\delta{}_\beta\, \eta_{\gamma\delta}. \tag{1}\] The matrix \(\Lambda\) has 16 entries. Both sides of (1) are symmetric in \(\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta\), so (1) is only \(4\cdot 5/2 = 10\) independent conditions, and a Lorentz transformation has \(16 - 10 = 6\) free parameters: three for rotations and three for boosts.
In special relativity one restricts to \(\Lambda^0{}_0 \geq 1\), the orthochronous transformations, which do not reverse the direction of time, and \(\det\Lambda = 1\), the proper ones, which do not change the handedness of space. The proper orthochronous Lorentz transformations form the group \(SO^+(1,3)\), whose double cover is \(SL(2, \mathbb C)\) [2].
crumbs: 3  Lorentz Transformations and Tensors

title: 3  Lorentz Transformations and Tensors
text:
ImportantProposition 3.1 (Two properties of Lorentz transformations). [1, Ch. 2]



Every Lorentz transformation satisfies \((\Lambda^0{}_0)^2 \geq 1\) and \((\det\Lambda)^2 = 1\).






NoteProof





The \(\alpha = \beta = 0\) component of (1) reads \[-1 = \Lambda^\gamma{}_0\, \Lambda^\delta{}_0\, \eta_{\gamma\delta} = -(\Lambda^0{}_0)^2 + \sum_{j=1}^3 (\Lambda^j{}_0)^2,\] so \((\Lambda^0{}_0)^2 = 1 + \sum_j (\Lambda^j{}_0)^2 \geq 1\). In matrix form (1) is \(\eta = \Lambda^T \eta\, \Lambda\), and taking determinants gives \(\det\eta = (\det\Lambda)^2 \det\eta\). \(\square\)

title: 3  Lorentz Transformations and Tensors
text:
Boosts
Let a test particle be at rest in the coordinates \(x^\alpha\) and move with velocity \(\vec v = d\vec x'/dt'\) in the coordinates \(x'^\alpha\). Along its path \(d\vec x = 0\), so \(dx'^i = \Lambda^i{}_0\, dt\) and \(dt' = \Lambda^0{}_0\, dt\), and the ratio gives \[\Lambda^i{}_0 = v^i\, \Lambda^0{}_0. \tag{2}\]






ImportantProposition 3.2 (The boost matrix). [1, Ch. 2]



The Lorentz transformation that takes a particle from rest to velocity \(\vec v\) can be taken to be \[\Lambda^0{}_0 = \gamma, \qquad \Lambda^i{}_0 = \Lambda^0{}_i = \gamma v^i, \qquad \Lambda^i{}_j = \delta^i_j + v^i v_j\, \frac{\gamma - 1}{v^2},\] where \(\gamma = (1 - v^2)^{-1/2}\).






NoteProof





Inserting (2) into the \(\alpha = \beta = 0\) component of (1) gives \(-1 = (\Lambda^0{}_0)^2(v^2 - 1)\), so \(\Lambda^0{}_0 = \gamma\) (taking the orthochronous root). The \((\alpha, \beta) = (i, 0)\) component gives \[0 = -\Lambda^0{}_i\, \Lambda^0{}_0 + \sum_j \Lambda^j{}_i\, \Lambda^j{}_0 = \gamma\Bigl(-\Lambda^0{}_i + \sum_j \Lambda^j{}_i\, v_j\Bigr),\] and the \((i, j)\) components give a quadratic condition on \(\Lambda^i{}_j\). One checks directly that the stated matrix satisfies all of these. \(\square\)





The spatial part \(\Lambda^i{}_j\) is not unique: if \(\Lambda\) takes a particle from rest to velocity \(\vec v\), so does \(\Lambda R\) for any rotation \(R\) (a rotation acts only on the spatial coordinates and preserves \(\eta_{\alpha\beta}\), so it is itself a Lorentz transformation).

title: 3  Lorentz Transformations and Tensors
section: Time dilation and the Doppler effect
text:
Time dilation and the Doppler effect
Let a clock be at rest in the frame \(\mathcal O\) and let \(dt'\) be the coordinate time between two ticks in the frame \(\mathcal O'\), in which the clock moves with speed \(v\). By Proposition 3.2, \(dt' = \gamma\, dt\). This alone does not yet say anything physical, since coordinate time is neither invariant nor directly observable. What observers measure is proper time. In \(\mathcal O\) the clock is at rest, so \[d\tau^2 = dt^2\Bigl(1 - \Bigl|\frac{d\vec x}{dt}\Bigr|^2\Bigr) = dt^2,\] and proper time and coordinate time agree. The interval \(dt'\) is measured by the clocks of \(\mathcal O'\), which are at rest in \(\mathcal O'\), so \(dt' = \gamma\, dt\) is a comparison of measured times: the moving clock runs slow, by the factor \(\gamma\).
Now replace the clock by a star emitting monochromatic light, and the ticks by successive wave crests. They are emitted a time \(dt' = \gamma\, dt\) apart. Between the two emissions the source moves a distance \(v_r\, dt'\) along the line of sight, where \(v_r\) is the component of \(\vec v\) away from the observer, so the crests arrive a time \((1 + v_r)\gamma\, dt\) apart.






ImportantProposition 3.3 (Relativistic Doppler effect). [1, Ch. 2]



The observed frequency \(\nu'\) and the emitted frequency \(\nu\) are related by \[\frac{\nu'}{\nu} = \underbrace{(1 + v_r)^{-1}}_{\text{Doppler}}\, \underbrace{(1 - v^2)^{1/2}}_{\text{time dilation}}.\] For motion along the line of sight, \(v_r = v\), this becomes \(\nu'/\nu = \sqrt{(1 - v)/(1 + v)} \approx 1 - v\) for small \(v\).


Measuring the shifts of spectral lines in starlight in this way gives the velocities of stars along the line of sight. The two effects are different in nature. The Doppler factor depends on the direction of motion and is already present in non-relativistic physics: it comes from the changing travel time of successive signals. Time dilation depends only on the speed.

title: 3  Lorentz Transformations and Tensors
text:
Vectors and tensors
Let \(x^\alpha \mapsto x'^\alpha = \Lambda^\alpha{}_\beta\, x^\beta\) be a Lorentz transformation and define \[\Lambda_\alpha{}^\beta = \eta_{\alpha\gamma}\, \eta^{\beta\delta}\, \Lambda^\gamma{}_\delta.\] Here \(\eta^{\alpha\beta}\) is the inverse of \(\eta_{\alpha\beta}\), \(\eta_{\alpha\gamma}\eta^{\gamma\beta} = \delta^\beta_\alpha\); numerically \(\eta^{\alpha\beta} = \eta_{\alpha\beta}\). From (1) it follows that \(\Lambda_\alpha{}^\gamma\, \Lambda^\alpha{}_\beta = \delta^\gamma_\beta\), so \(\Lambda_\alpha{}^\beta\) is the inverse transformation.






NoteDefinition 3.4 (Lorentz vectors and tensors). [1, Ch. 2]



A contravariant vector transforms as \(V'^\alpha = \Lambda^\alpha{}_\beta\, V^\beta\), and a covariant vector as \(U'_\alpha = \Lambda_\alpha{}^\beta\, U_\beta\). More generally, a tensor is an object with upper and lower indices, each of which transforms in this way; for example \[T'^\gamma{}_{\alpha\beta} = \Lambda^\gamma{}_\delta\, \Lambda_\alpha{}^\epsilon\, \Lambda_\beta{}^\zeta\, T^\delta{}_{\epsilon\zeta}.\]


Note that “covariant” here describes how an object transforms; a covariant equation (Definition 1.4) is one whose two sides transform in the same way. Not everything with indices is a tensor: the affine connection of Definition 1.11 does not obey a transformation law of this form.
The contraction of a covariant with a contravariant vector is a scalar: \[U'_\alpha V'^\alpha = \Lambda_\alpha{}^\beta\, \Lambda^\alpha{}_\gamma\, U_\beta V^\gamma = \delta^\beta_\gamma\, U_\beta V^\gamma = U_\beta V^\beta.\]






CautionExample 3.5 (Derivatives).



By the chain rule, \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x'^\alpha} = \dfrac{\partial x^\beta}{\partial x'^\alpha}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x^\beta} = \Lambda_\alpha{}^\beta\, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x^\beta}\), so the gradient is a covariant vector. Contracting two of them gives the d’Alembertian \[\Box = \eta^{\alpha\beta}\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^\alpha}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\beta} = \nabla^2 - \frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2},\] which is a scalar operator.








ImportantProposition 3.6 (Tensor algebra). [1, Ch. 2]




Linear combinations \(a R^\alpha{}_\beta + b S^\alpha{}_\beta\) of tensors of the same type are tensors.
Direct products, such as \(A^\alpha{}_\beta\, B^\gamma\), are tensors.
Contracting an upper with a lower index gives a tensor; in particular indices can be raised and lowered with \(\eta\), for example \(T^\alpha{}_\beta{}^{\gamma\beta} = \eta^{\beta\delta}\, T^\alpha{}_\beta{}^\gamma{}_\delta\).
Derivatives \(\partial_\alpha T^{\beta\gamma}\) are tensors under Lorentz transformations, but not under general coordinate transformations; this is what the covariant derivative of Lecture 7 will fix.



Examples of Lorentz tensors are the metric \(\eta_{\alpha\beta}\), which is invariant by (1), the zero tensor, and the totally antisymmetric Levi-Civita symbol \(\epsilon^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\). The latter is a tensor under proper Lorentz transformations only; under general coordinate transformations it is a tensor density (Lecture 8).
The point of tensors is that a tensor equation which holds in one frame holds in all. If \(T^\alpha{}_\beta = S^\alpha{}_\beta\) in the coordinates \((t, \vec x)\), then \[T'^\alpha{}_\beta = \Lambda^\alpha{}_\gamma\, \Lambda_\beta{}^\epsilon\, T^\gamma{}_\epsilon = \Lambda^\alpha{}_\gamma\, \Lambda_\beta{}^\epsilon\, S^\gamma{}_\epsilon = S'^\alpha{}_\beta\] in the coordinates \((t', \vec x')\).

title: 4  Particle Mechanics in Special Relativity
text:
Four-force and four-momentum
To extend Newton’s second law to relativistic speeds, we define the four-force on a test particle by \[f^\alpha = m\, \frac{d^2x^\alpha}{d\tau^2}, \tag{1}\] evaluated at the point \((t_0, \vec x(t_0))\) on its trajectory. Since \(m\) and \(d\tau\) are invariant, \(f^\alpha\) is a contravariant vector. Moreover, given the point and the velocity \(\vec v = d\vec x/dt\) there, the boost \(\Lambda(-\vec v)\) of Proposition 3.2 takes us to coordinates \(x'^\alpha\) in which the particle is momentarily at rest: \[\frac{dx'^i}{dt'} = 0, \qquad d\tau^2 = dt'^2\Bigl(1 - \Bigl|\frac{d\vec x'}{dt'}\Bigr|^2\Bigr) = dt'^2 \quad \text{at } t' = t'_0.\] In these coordinates (1) reads \(f'^0 = 0\) and \(f'^i = m\, d^2x'^i/dt'^2 = F^i\), the ordinary Newtonian force. The four-force is thus fixed by the Newtonian force in the rest frame.
Using \(d\tau = \gamma^{-1} dt\), \[p^0 = m\gamma = m + \tfrac12 m v^2 + \mathcal O(v^4) = E, \qquad p^i = m\gamma v^i = m v^i + \mathcal O(v^3),\] the rest energy plus kinetic energy, and the Newtonian momentum. For a photon \(d\tau = 0\) and the definition breaks down, but the ratio \(v^i = p^i/p^0\) still makes sense.

title: 4  Particle Mechanics in Special Relativity
text:
TipRemark 4.1 (Why proper time?).



Parametrising a worldline \(X(\tau)\) by proper time makes the four-velocity \(U = dX/d\tau = \gamma(1, \vec v)\) transform simply, \(U' = \Lambda U\), because \(d\tau\) is invariant. Had we used \(dX/dt\) instead, both \(X\) and \(t\) would transform, and the result would not be a vector.








NoteDefinition 4.2 (Four-momentum). [1, Ch. 2]



The energy-momentum four-vector of a particle of mass \(m\) is \[p^\alpha = m\, \frac{dx^\alpha}{d\tau}.\]









ImportantProposition 4.3 (Mass shell). [1, Ch. 2]



The four-velocity and four-momentum of a massive particle satisfy \[\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, U^\alpha U^\beta = -1, \qquad \eta_{\alpha\beta}\, p^\alpha p^\beta = -m^2, \qquad E^2 = |\vec p|^2 + m^2.\]






NoteProof





Dividing \(d\tau^2 = -\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, dx^\alpha dx^\beta\) by \(d\tau^2\) gives \(\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, U^\alpha U^\beta = -1\), and multiplying by \(m^2\) gives \(\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, p^\alpha p^\beta = -m^2\). On the other hand \(\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, p^\alpha p^\beta = -(p^0)^2 + |\vec p|^2\), and with \(p^0 = E\) the last identity follows. Both contractions are scalars, so they hold in every inertial frame. \(\square\)

title: 4  Particle Mechanics in Special Relativity
text:
The energy-momentum tensor
Consider a set of particles labelled by \(n\), with \(x_n^0(t) = t\). The density of four-momentum is \[T^{\alpha 0}(x) = \sum_n p_n^\alpha(t)\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)),\] with units of momentum per volume, since the delta function has units of inverse volume. The current of four-momentum is \[T^{\alpha i}(x) = \sum_n p_n^\alpha(t)\, \frac{dx_n^i}{dt}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)),\] with units of momentum per area per time.






NoteDefinition 4.4 (Energy-momentum tensor of point particles). [1, Ch. 2]



The energy-momentum tensor of a system of point particles is \[T^{\alpha\beta}(x) = \sum_n p_n^\alpha(t)\, \frac{dx_n^\beta}{dt}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)). \tag{2}\]








ImportantProposition 4.5 (Symmetry and tensor character). [1, Ch. 2]



\(T^{\alpha\beta}\) is symmetric and is a Lorentz tensor.






NoteProof





Since \(p_n^\alpha = m\, dx_n^\alpha/d\tau\) and \(E_n = p_n^0 = m\, dt/d\tau\), we have \(dx_n^\beta/dt = p_n^\beta/E_n\), and \[T^{\alpha\beta}(x) = \sum_n \frac{p_n^\alpha\, p_n^\beta}{E_n}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)),\] which is manifestly symmetric.
For the tensor property, write the three-dimensional delta function as an integral over a four-dimensional one, \(\delta^{(4)}(x - x_n(t)) = \delta(x^0 - t)\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t))\), and change variables to proper time: \[T^{\alpha\beta}(x) = \sum_n \int dt\, p_n^\alpha\, \frac{dx_n^\beta}{dt}\, \delta^{(4)}(x - x_n(t)) = \sum_n \int d\tau\, p_n^\alpha\, \frac{dx_n^\beta}{d\tau}\, \delta^{(4)}(x - x_n(\tau)).\] The four-dimensional delta function is a Lorentz scalar: \(\int d^4x\, \delta^{(4)}(x) = 1\) and \(d^4x\) is invariant because \(\det\Lambda = 1\). So \(T^{\alpha\beta}\) is a product of two contravariant vectors integrated against a scalar. Note that this argument fails for the three-dimensional delta function, and for general coordinate transformations, whose Jacobian need not be one. \(\square\)





The symmetry of \(T^{\alpha\beta}\) says that the flux of the \(\alpha\)-component of momentum across a surface of constant \(x^\beta\) equals the flux of the \(\beta\)-component across a surface of constant \(x^\alpha\). It is what makes angular momentum conserved, as we see below.






ImportantProposition 4.6 (Conservation of energy and momentum). [1, Ch. 2]



If the particles are free, or interact only in collisions localised at points (in which four-momentum is conserved), then \[\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\beta}\, T^{\alpha\beta} = 0. \tag{3}\] If the particles are acted on by four-forces \(f_n^\alpha\), then instead \(\partial_\beta T^{\alpha\beta} = G^\alpha\) with \[G^\alpha(x) = \sum_n \frac{d\tau_n}{dt}\, f_n^\alpha\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)).\]






NoteProof





Since \(\partial_{x^i}\delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n) = -\partial_{x_n^i}\delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n)\), \[\begin{aligned}
\partial_i T^{\alpha i} &= -\sum_n p_n^\alpha\, \frac{dx_n^i}{dt}\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x_n^i}\delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)) = -\sum_n p_n^\alpha\, \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)) \\
&= -\partial_0 T^{\alpha 0} + \sum_n \frac{dp_n^\alpha}{dt}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)).
\end{aligned}\] For free particles \(dp_n^\alpha/dt = 0\); with localised collisions the sum of the changes vanishes at each collision point. Otherwise \(dp_n^\alpha/dt = (d\tau_n/dt) f_n^\alpha\), which gives \(G^\alpha\). \(\square\)





The energy-momentum tensor is the conserved Noether current of spacetime translations \(x^\alpha \mapsto x^\alpha + a^\alpha\) (see Invariance and conservation in my notes on Noether’s theorem): its time components express conservation of energy and its space components conservation of momentum.






ImportantProposition 4.7 (Total four-momentum). [1, Ch. 2]



If \(T^{\alpha\beta}\) vanishes at spatial infinity, the total four-momentum \[p^\alpha_{\text{tot}} = \int d^3x\, T^{\alpha 0}(x)\] is conserved.






NoteProof





By (3) and the divergence theorem, \[\frac{dp^\alpha_{\text{tot}}}{dt} = \int d^3x\, \partial_0 T^{\alpha 0} = -\int d^3x\, \partial_i T^{\alpha i} = 0. \qquad \square\]

title: 4  Particle Mechanics in Special Relativity
text:
Angular momentum and spin






NoteDefinition 4.8 (Angular momentum). [1, Ch. 2]



The angular momentum density and the total angular momentum are \[M^{\gamma\alpha\beta} = x^\alpha T^{\beta\gamma} - x^\beta T^{\alpha\gamma}, \qquad J^{\alpha\beta} = \int d^3x\, M^{0\alpha\beta}.\]


Using (3), \(\partial_\gamma M^{\gamma\alpha\beta} = T^{\beta\alpha} - T^{\alpha\beta} = 0\) by Proposition 4.5. Since \(M^{\gamma\alpha\beta}\) is antisymmetric in \(\alpha\beta\), these are six continuity equations, and \(J^{\alpha\beta}\) is conserved.
Of these six, the components \(J^{0i} = t\, p^i_{\text{tot}} - \int d^3x\, x^i T^{00}\) carry no new information: choosing the origin so that \(\int d^3x\, x^i T^{00} = 0\) at \(t = 0\) makes \(J^{0i}\) vanish then, and hence at all times, since \(p^i_{\text{tot}}\) is conserved. The physical components are \[J^{ij} = \int d^3x\, \bigl(x^i T^{j0} - x^j T^{i0}\bigr),\] which have the structure of \(L_i = \epsilon_{ijk}\, x_j p_k\): we identify \((J^{23}, J^{31}, J^{12})\) with the three components of angular momentum. \(J\) contains both an orbital and an intrinsic part.
Under a translation \(x^\alpha \mapsto x^\alpha + a^\alpha\), \[J^{\alpha\beta} \mapsto J^{\alpha\beta} + a^\alpha p^\beta_{\text{tot}} - a^\beta p^\alpha_{\text{tot}}, \tag{4}\] since orbital angular momentum is defined with respect to a centre of rotation. The intrinsic part should not depend on that choice.






NoteDefinition 4.9 (Spin). [1, Ch. 2]



The spin four-vector is \[S_\alpha = \tfrac12\, \epsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\, J^{\beta\gamma}\, U^\delta, \qquad U^\delta = \frac{p^\delta_{\text{tot}}}{\sqrt{-\eta_{\mu\nu}\, p^\mu_{\text{tot}}\, p^\nu_{\text{tot}}}},\] where \(U^\delta\) is the four-velocity of the centre of mass.








ImportantProposition 4.10 (Properties of spin). [1, Ch. 2]



\(S_\alpha\) is invariant under translations and satisfies \(S_\alpha U^\alpha = 0\). In the centre-of-mass frame, \(U = (1, 0, 0, 0)\), it is \(S = (0, J^{23}, J^{31}, J^{12})\).






NoteProof





By (4), a translation adds to \(S_\alpha\) terms proportional to \(\epsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\, a^\beta U^\gamma U^\delta\) (since \(p_{\text{tot}} \propto U\)), which vanish because \(\epsilon\) is antisymmetric and \(U^\gamma U^\delta\) symmetric in \(\gamma\delta\). The same argument gives \(S_\alpha U^\alpha \propto \epsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\, J^{\beta\gamma} U^\delta U^\alpha = 0\). In the centre-of-mass frame only \(\delta = 0\) contributes, and the components can be read off. \(\square\)

title: 4  Particle Mechanics in Special Relativity
text:
Charges and currents
The same construction applies to electric charge. The charge density, the current density and the four-current of a set of particles with charges \(e_n\) are \[\varepsilon(x) = \sum_n e_n\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)), \qquad \vec j(x) = \sum_n e_n\, \frac{d\vec x_n}{dt}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)),\] \[J^\alpha(x) = \sum_n e_n\, \frac{dx_n^\alpha}{dt}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)), \qquad x_n^0 = t,\] so that \(J^\alpha = (\varepsilon, \vec j)\). Charge is never created or destroyed, and the argument of Proposition 4.6, with \(p_n^\alpha\) replaced by the constants \(e_n\), gives \[\partial_\alpha J^\alpha = 0.\] Hence the total charge \(Q = \int d^3x\, J^0\) is constant in time. The electromagnetic field itself is the subject of the next lecture.

title: 5  Electrodynamics and the Affine Connection
text:
Charge is a scalar
In Lecture 4 we introduced the four-current \(J^\alpha\) of a set of charged particles, with \[\partial_\alpha J^\alpha = 0, \qquad Q = \int d^3x\, J^0(x). \tag{1}\] By the divergence theorem \(dQ/dt = -\int d^3x\, \partial_i J^i = 0\), so \(Q\) is constant in time. It is also the same in every inertial frame.
The same argument, applied to each component of \(T^{\alpha 0}\), shows that the total four-momentum \(p^\alpha_{\text{tot}}\) of Proposition 4.7 is a contravariant vector.
crumbs: 5  Electrodynamics and the Affine Connection

title: 5  Electrodynamics and the Affine Connection
text:
ImportantProposition 5.1 (Charge is Lorentz invariant). [1, Ch. 2]



The total charge \(Q\) is a Lorentz scalar.






NoteProof





Let \(n_\beta = (1, 0, 0, 0)\) and let \(\theta\) be the step function, so that \(\partial_t\theta(t) = \delta(t)\). Then \[Q = \int d^4x\, J^\alpha(x)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^\alpha}\theta(n_\beta x^\beta),\] since the derivative produces \(\delta(t)\) and reduces the integral to one over \(t = 0\). In the transformed frame the same expression holds with \(n_\beta\) replaced by \(n'_\gamma = n_\beta\Lambda^\beta{}_\gamma\), the normal of the surface \(t' = 0\). Hence \[Q' - Q = \int d^4x\, J^\alpha\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^\alpha}\bigl[\theta(n'_\beta x^\beta) - \theta(n_\beta x^\beta)\bigr] = -\int d^4x\, \bigl(\partial_\alpha J^\alpha\bigr)\bigl[\theta(n'_\beta x^\beta) - \theta(n_\beta x^\beta)\bigr] = 0,\] integrating by parts and using (1). The boundary term vanishes because the bracket is non-zero only between the two surfaces \(t = 0\) and \(t' = 0\) (Figure 5.1), and the current vanishes at spatial infinity, where the two surfaces separate. \(\square\)











Figure 5.1: The surfaces \(t = 0\) and \(t' = 0\) of two inertial frames. The current is localised, so the region between the surfaces where it is non-zero is bounded, and the two integrals of \(J^0\) agree.

title: 5  Electrodynamics and the Affine Connection
text:
Maxwell’s equations in covariant form
In units with \(\epsilon_0 = \mu_0 = 1\), Maxwell’s equations read \[\nabla\cdot\vec E = \varepsilon, \qquad \nabla\times\vec B = \vec j + \frac{\partial\vec E}{\partial t}, \qquad \nabla\cdot\vec B = 0, \qquad \nabla\times\vec E = -\frac{\partial\vec B}{\partial t}. \tag{2}\]






NoteDefinition 5.2 (Field strength tensor). [1, Ch. 2]



The electromagnetic field strength tensor is the antisymmetric tensor with \(F^{0i} = E_i\) and \(F^{ij} = \epsilon_{ijk} B_k\): \[F^{\alpha\beta} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & E_1 & E_2 & E_3 \\ -E_1 & 0 & B_3 & -B_2 \\ -E_2 & -B_3 & 0 & B_1 \\ -E_3 & B_2 & -B_1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\]








ImportantProposition 5.3 (Covariant Maxwell equations). [1, Ch. 2]



Maxwell’s equations (2) are equivalent to \[\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\alpha} F^{\alpha\beta} = -J^\beta, \qquad \epsilon^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^\beta} F_{\gamma\delta} = 0. \tag{3}\] The second equation is equivalent to \[\partial_\alpha F_{\beta\gamma} + \partial_\beta F_{\gamma\alpha} + \partial_\gamma F_{\alpha\beta} = 0. \tag{4}\]






NoteProof





For \(\beta = 0\) the first equation is \(\partial_i F^{i0} = -\partial_i E_i = -J^0\), which is Gauss’s law. For \(\beta = j\) it is \(\partial_0 F^{0j} + \partial_i F^{ij} = \partial_t E_j - (\nabla\times\vec B)_j = -j_j\), which is the Ampère–Maxwell law; here \(\partial_i F^{ij} = \epsilon_{ijk}\partial_i B_k = -(\nabla\times\vec B)_j\). The second equation contains the two homogeneous laws in the same way: \(\alpha = 0\) gives \(\nabla\cdot\vec B = 0\) and \(\alpha = i\) gives Faraday’s law. Equation (4) is trivial unless \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) are distinct, and then it is a component of the second equation in (3). \(\square\)





Equation (4) contains more equations than the second equation in (3), but the extra ones are trivial. Its advantage is that it generalises directly to general relativity (Lecture 8).






ImportantProposition 5.4 (Lorentz force). [1, Ch. 2]



The four-force on a particle of charge \(e\) in an electromagnetic field is \[f^\alpha = e\, F^\alpha{}_\gamma\, \frac{dx^\gamma}{d\tau} = e\, \eta_{\beta\gamma}\, F^{\alpha\beta}\, \frac{dx^\gamma}{d\tau}.\]






NoteProof





Both sides are contravariant vectors, so it suffices to check the equation in one frame. As in Lecture 4, boost to coordinates \(x'^\alpha\) in which the particle is momentarily at rest, so that \(dx'^\gamma/d\tau = \delta^\gamma_0\). Then \(f'^0 = e F'^0{}_0 = 0\) and \(f'^i = e\, F'^i{}_0 = e\, \eta_{00} F'^{i0} = e E'_i\), the Coulomb force, which is the correct force on a charge at rest. \(\square\)

title: 5  Electrodynamics and the Affine Connection
section: The affine connection and the metric
text:
The affine connection and the metric
We return to gravity. Let \(X\) be a spacetime point and \(\xi^\alpha_X\) a locally inertial coordinate system at \(X\). By Definition 1.11, \[\frac{\partial^2\xi^\alpha_X}{\partial x^\mu \partial x^\nu} = \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\, \frac{\partial\xi^\alpha_X}{\partial x^\lambda}.\] Read this as a differential equation for \(\xi^\alpha_X(x)\), given \(\Gamma\). Expanding around \(X\), \[\xi^\alpha_X(x) = a^\alpha + b^\alpha{}_\mu\, (x - X)^\mu + \tfrac12\, b^\alpha{}_\lambda\, \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}(X)\, (x - X)^\mu (x - X)^\nu + \cdots,\] with \(a^\alpha = \xi^\alpha_X(X)\) and \(b^\alpha{}_\mu = \partial\xi^\alpha_X/\partial x^\mu|_{x = X}\). The metric fixes \(g_{\mu\nu}(X) = \eta_{\alpha\beta}\, b^\alpha{}_\mu\, b^\beta{}_\nu\), which is 10 conditions on the 16 entries of \(b\). This leaves 6 free parameters in \(b\) and 4 in \(a\): the 10 parameters of a Poincaré transformation. Locally inertial coordinates thus exist and are unique up to Poincaré transformations, as they should be.






ImportantProposition 5.5 (The connection is determined by the metric). [1, Ch. 3]



The affine connection is given by \[\Gamma^\sigma_{\lambda\mu} = \tfrac12\, g^{\sigma\nu}\Bigl(\frac{\partial g_{\mu\nu}}{\partial x^\lambda} + \frac{\partial g_{\lambda\nu}}{\partial x^\mu} - \frac{\partial g_{\mu\lambda}}{\partial x^\nu}\Bigr). \tag{5}\]






NoteProof





Differentiating \(g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\alpha\beta}\, \partial_\mu\xi^\alpha\, \partial_\nu\xi^\beta\) and using Definition 1.11 for the second derivatives, \[\frac{\partial g_{\mu\nu}}{\partial x^\lambda} = \Gamma^\rho_{\lambda\mu}\, g_{\rho\nu} + \Gamma^\rho_{\lambda\nu}\, g_{\mu\rho}.\] Adding the same identity with \(\lambda \leftrightarrow \mu\) and subtracting it with \(\lambda \to \nu\), \(\nu \to \lambda\), and using \(\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\nu} = \Gamma^\rho_{\nu\mu}\), all terms cancel except \[\frac{\partial g_{\mu\nu}}{\partial x^\lambda} + \frac{\partial g_{\lambda\nu}}{\partial x^\mu} - \frac{\partial g_{\mu\lambda}}{\partial x^\nu} = 2\, \Gamma^\rho_{\lambda\mu}\, g_{\rho\nu}.\] Multiplying by \(g^{\sigma\nu}\) gives (5). \(\square\)





At \(X\) one can therefore always pass to coordinates in which \(g_{\mu\nu}(X) = \eta_{\mu\nu}\) and \(\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}(X) = 0\). This rests on the equivalence principle, which guarantees that locally inertial coordinates exist.
crumbs: 5  Electrodynamics and the Affine Connection

title: 5  Electrodynamics and the Affine Connection
section: Free fall of massive and massless particles
text:
Free fall of massive and massless particles
For a massive particle, the derivation in Lecture 1 gave the following.






NoteDefinition 5.6 (Geodesic equation). [1, Ch. 3]



The geodesic equation is \[\frac{d^2x^\lambda}{d\tau^2} + \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\, \frac{dx^\mu}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\nu}{d\tau} = 0, \qquad d\tau^2 = -g_{\mu\nu}\, dx^\mu dx^\nu. \tag{6}\]


A massless particle has no proper time, \(d\tau = 0\). In locally inertial coordinates it still moves on a straight line, \(d^2\xi^\alpha/d\sigma^2 = 0\) with \(\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, (d\xi^\alpha/d\sigma)(d\xi^\beta/d\sigma) = 0\), for a parameter \(\sigma\) such as \(\sigma = \xi^0\); the solutions are \(\xi^i(\sigma) = A^i\sigma + B^i\). The same change of coordinates then gives \[\frac{d^2x^\lambda}{d\sigma^2} + \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\, \frac{dx^\mu}{d\sigma}\frac{dx^\nu}{d\sigma} = 0, \qquad g_{\mu\nu}\, \frac{dx^\mu}{d\sigma}\frac{dx^\nu}{d\sigma} = 0. \tag{7}\] Writing out the second condition, \(g_{00}\, dt^2 + 2g_{0i}\, dt\, dx^i + g_{ij}\, dx^i dx^j = 0\), and solving for \(dt\), \[dt = \frac{1}{g_{00}}\Bigl\{-g_{0i}\, dx^i - \bigl[(g_{0i}\, g_{0j} - g_{00}\, g_{ij})\, dx^i dx^j\bigr]^{1/2}\Bigr\},\] the sign chosen so that \(dt > 0\) (recall \(g_{00} < 0\)). If the metric is static, the coordinate time a light signal takes between two given points is therefore the same for every signal. We use this in the next lecture.

title: 6  The Newtonian Limit and Gravitational Redshift
text:
The Newtonian limit
The geodesic equation (6) of Lecture 5 should reduce to Newton’s law of gravity for slow particles in weak, static fields. We assume:
crumbs: 6  The Newtonian Limit and Gravitational Redshift

title: 6  The Newtonian Limit and Gravitational Redshift
text:
the particle is slow, \(|d\vec x/dt| \ll 1\);
the field is static, \(\partial_0 g_{\mu\nu} = 0\);
the field is weak, \(g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\mu\nu} + h_{\mu\nu}\) with \(|h_{\mu\nu}| \ll 1\).







ImportantProposition 6.1 (Newtonian limit). [1, Ch. 3]



Under assumptions 1–3, the geodesic equation reduces to \[\frac{d^2\vec x}{dt^2} = \tfrac12\, \nabla h_{00},\] which is Newton’s law \(d^2\vec x/dt^2 = -\nabla\phi\) provided \[g_{00} = -(1 + 2\phi). \tag{1}\]






NoteProof





By assumption 1, \(|d\vec x/d\tau| \ll dt/d\tau\), so only the \(\mu = \nu = 0\) term of the connection survives: \[\frac{d^2x^\mu}{d\tau^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{00}\Bigl(\frac{dt}{d\tau}\Bigr)^2 = 0.\] By assumption 2 and (5) of Lecture 5, \[\Gamma^\mu_{00} = -\tfrac12\, g^{\mu\sigma}\, \partial_\sigma g_{00} = -\tfrac12\, g^{\mu i}\, \partial_i g_{00}.\] By assumption 3, \(\partial_i g_{00} = \partial_i h_{00}\) is of order \(h\). For \(\mu = 0\), \(g^{0i}\) is also of order \(h\), so the second term is of second order and \(d^2t/d\tau^2 = 0\): \(dt/d\tau\) is constant. For \(\mu = i\) we may replace \(g^{ij}\) by \(\delta^{ij}\), and \[\frac{d^2x^i}{d\tau^2} = \tfrac12\, \partial_i h_{00}\Bigl(\frac{dt}{d\tau}\Bigr)^2.\] Dividing by the constant \((dt/d\tau)^2\) gives the stated equation. Comparing with Newton’s law, \(h_{00} = -2\phi + \text{const}\). Far from all sources \(\phi \to 0\) and \(g_{\mu\nu} \to \eta_{\mu\nu}\), so the constant is zero. \(\square\)

title: 6  The Newtonian Limit and Gravitational Redshift
text:
Gravitational redshift
Let an atom at rest emit light of a definite frequency. In locally inertial coordinates at the atom, the proper time \(\Delta\tau\) between two wave crests is fixed by atomic physics. In arbitrary coordinates, \[\Delta\tau = \bigl(-\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, d\xi^\alpha_X\, d\xi^\beta_X\bigr)^{1/2} = \bigl(-g_{\mu\nu}(X)\, dx^\mu dx^\nu\bigr)^{1/2},\] so the coordinate time between the crests is \[dt = \Delta\tau\, \Bigl(-g_{\mu\nu}\, \frac{dx^\mu}{dt}\frac{dx^\nu}{dt}\Bigr)^{-1/2} = \Delta\tau\, \bigl(-g_{00}\bigr)^{-1/2}\] for a source at rest.
Now let the atom sit at \(x_2\), say on the surface of the Sun, and the observer at \(x_1\), on the Earth (Figure 6.1). The crests leave \(x_2\) a coordinate time \(dt_2 = \Delta\tau\, (-g_{00}(x_2))^{-1/2}\) apart. In a static field every light signal takes the same coordinate time to travel from \(x_2\) to \(x_1\) (Lecture 5), so they also arrive \(dt_2\) apart. The observer at rest at \(x_1\) measures the proper time \(\sqrt{-g_{00}(x_1)}\, dt_2\) between them, so the observed frequency is \[\nu_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{-g_{00}(x_1)}\, dt_2}.\] The same atom at rest at \(x_1\) is seen with frequency \(\nu_1 = 1/(\sqrt{-g_{00}(x_1)}\, dt_1)\), with \(dt_1 = \Delta\tau\, (-g_{00}(x_1))^{-1/2}\).






Figure 6.1: Light emitted at the surface of the Sun, deep in its potential well, climbs out to the Earth. The crests leave and arrive the same coordinate time apart, but clocks deeper in the well run slower, so the light arrives redshifted.









ImportantProposition 6.2 (Gravitational redshift). [1, Ch. 3]



The ratio of the frequency of light emitted at \(x_2\) to that of the same line emitted at \(x_1\), both observed at \(x_1\), is \[\frac{\nu_2}{\nu_1} = \frac{dt_1}{dt_2} = \Bigl(\frac{g_{00}(x_2)}{g_{00}(x_1)}\Bigr)^{1/2}.\] In a weak field, by (1), \[\frac{\nu_2}{\nu_1} = \Bigl(\frac{1 + 2\phi(x_2)}{1 + 2\phi(x_1)}\Bigr)^{1/2} \approx 1 + \phi(x_2) - \phi(x_1).\]








CautionExample 6.3 (Light from the Sun).



For a line emitted on the Sun and observed on the Earth, \[\frac{\nu_2}{\nu_1} - 1 \approx \phi_\odot - \phi_\oplus \approx \phi_\odot = -\frac{GM_\odot}{R_\odot} \approx -2.12\times 10^{-6},\] since the Earth’s potential is much smaller. The frequency decreases and the wavelength increases: the light is redshifted.

Tensors under general coordinate transformations
We now want tools for writing equations that are covariant under arbitrary coordinate transformations \(x^\mu \mapsto x'^\mu\). The definitions mirror those for Lorentz transformations (Definition 3.4), with \(\Lambda\) replaced by the Jacobian of the transformation.






NoteDefinition 6.4 (Scalars and vectors). [1, Ch. 4]



Under \(x^\mu \mapsto x'^\mu\):

a scalar transforms as \(S' = S\);
a contravariant vector transforms as \(V'^\mu = \dfrac{\partial x'^\mu}{\partial x^\nu}\, V^\nu\), the example being the differential \(dx^\mu\);
a covariant vector transforms as \(U'_\mu = \dfrac{\partial x^\nu}{\partial x'^\mu}\, U_\nu\), the example being the gradient \(\partial\phi/\partial x^\mu\) of a scalar.

title: 7  Derivatives of Tensors
text:
Tensor densities
An equation is generally covariant if it takes the same form in all coordinate systems: \(S^\mu = T^\mu\) if and only if \(S'^\mu = T'^\mu\). Tensors under general coordinate transformations (Definition 6.4) give generally covariant equations in the same way as Lorentz tensors gave Lorentz covariant ones. This lecture collects the objects that are not quite tensors, and shows how to differentiate tensors so that the result is again a tensor.
The Levi-Civita symbol \(\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\) is another example. Under proper Lorentz transformations it is a tensor; under improper ones it picks up a sign and is called a pseudotensor; under general coordinate transformations it is a tensor density.

title: 7  Derivatives of Tensors
text:
NoteDefinition 7.1 (Tensor density). [1, Ch. 4]



A scalar density of weight \(W\) transforms as \[S' = \Bigl|\frac{\partial x'}{\partial x}\Bigr|^W S,\] where \(|\partial x'/\partial x|\) is the Jacobian determinant. A tensor density of weight \(W\) transforms like a tensor, times the same factor.








CautionExample 7.2 (The determinant of the metric).



Since \(g'_{\mu\nu} = \frac{\partial x^\rho}{\partial x'^\mu}\frac{\partial x^\sigma}{\partial x'^\nu}\, g_{\rho\sigma}\), taking determinants gives \[\det g'_{\mu\nu} = \Bigl|\frac{\partial x}{\partial x'}\Bigr|^2 \det g_{\mu\nu},\] so \(g := -\det g_{\mu\nu}\) is a scalar density of weight \(-2\). Since \(d^4x' = |\partial x'/\partial x|\, d^4x\), the volume element \(\sqrt g\, d^4x\) is invariant. This is how integrals are made generally covariant.

title: 7  Derivatives of Tensors
section: The connection is not a tensor
text:
The connection is not a tensor






ImportantProposition 7.3 (Transformation of the connection). [1, Ch. 4]



Under a general coordinate transformation, \[\Gamma'^\lambda_{\mu\nu} = \frac{\partial x'^\lambda}{\partial x^\rho}\frac{\partial x^\sigma}{\partial x'^\mu}\frac{\partial x^\tau}{\partial x'^\nu}\, \Gamma^\rho_{\sigma\tau} - \frac{\partial^2 x'^\lambda}{\partial x^\sigma \partial x^\rho}\frac{\partial x^\sigma}{\partial x'^\mu}\frac{\partial x^\rho}{\partial x'^\nu}. \tag{1}\] The second term means that \(\Gamma\) is not a tensor.






NoteProof





By Definition 1.11 and the chain rule, \[\Gamma'^\lambda_{\mu\nu} = \frac{\partial x'^\lambda}{\partial\xi^\alpha}\frac{\partial^2\xi^\alpha}{\partial x'^\mu \partial x'^\nu} = \Bigl(\frac{\partial x'^\lambda}{\partial x^\rho}\frac{\partial x^\rho}{\partial\xi^\alpha}\Bigr)\frac{\partial x^\sigma}{\partial x'^\mu}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\sigma}\Bigl(\frac{\partial x^\tau}{\partial x'^\nu}\frac{\partial\xi^\alpha}{\partial x^\tau}\Bigr).\] The derivative acts on both factors in the bracket. Acting on the second it gives the first term of (1); acting on the first it gives \(\frac{\partial x'^\lambda}{\partial x^\rho}\frac{\partial^2 x^\rho}{\partial x'^\mu \partial x'^\nu}\). Differentiating \(\frac{\partial x'^\lambda}{\partial x^\rho}\frac{\partial x^\rho}{\partial x'^\nu} = \delta^\lambda_\nu\) with respect to \(x'^\mu\) gives \[\frac{\partial x'^\lambda}{\partial x^\rho}\frac{\partial^2 x^\rho}{\partial x'^\mu \partial x'^\nu} = -\frac{\partial x^\sigma}{\partial x'^\mu}\frac{\partial x^\rho}{\partial x'^\nu}\frac{\partial^2 x'^\lambda}{\partial x^\sigma \partial x^\rho},\] which is the second term of (1). \(\square\)





The acceleration \(d^2x^\mu/d\tau^2\) is not a vector either: \[\frac{d^2x'^\mu}{d\tau^2} = \frac{\partial x'^\mu}{\partial x^\nu}\frac{d^2x^\nu}{d\tau^2} + \frac{\partial^2 x'^\mu}{\partial x^\sigma \partial x^\nu}\frac{dx^\sigma}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\nu}{d\tau}.\] The extra term has the opposite sign of the one in (1), so it cancels in the combination \[\frac{d^2x^\mu}{d\tau^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}\, \frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\sigma}{d\tau},\] which is therefore a vector. The geodesic equation (Definition 5.6) is generally covariant, although it is built from two pieces that are not.

title: 7  Derivatives of Tensors
text:
The covariant derivative
The partial derivative of a vector is not a tensor: \[\frac{\partial V'^\mu}{\partial x'^\nu} = \frac{\partial x^\rho}{\partial x'^\nu}\frac{\partial x'^\mu}{\partial x^\sigma}\frac{\partial V^\sigma}{\partial x^\rho} + \frac{\partial x^\rho}{\partial x'^\nu}\frac{\partial^2 x'^\mu}{\partial x^\rho \partial x^\sigma}\, V^\sigma.\] Again, the second term is cancelled by the inhomogeneous term in (1).






NoteDefinition 7.4 (Covariant derivative). [1, Ch. 4]



The covariant derivatives of a contravariant and a covariant vector are \[V^\mu{}_{;\nu} = \frac{\partial V^\mu}{\partial x^\nu} + \Gamma^\mu_{\nu\rho}\, V^\rho, \qquad U_{\mu;\nu} = \frac{\partial U_\mu}{\partial x^\nu} - \Gamma^\sigma_{\mu\nu}\, U_\sigma.\] For a general tensor there is one term for each index, with a plus sign for upper and a minus sign for lower indices, for example \[T^{\mu\gamma}{}_{\lambda;\rho} = \frac{\partial T^{\mu\gamma}{}_\lambda}{\partial x^\rho} + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\eta}\, T^{\eta\gamma}{}_\lambda + \Gamma^\gamma_{\rho\eta}\, T^{\mu\eta}{}_\lambda - \Gamma^\eta_{\lambda\rho}\, T^{\mu\gamma}{}_\eta.\]


By construction \(V'^\mu{}_{;\nu} = \frac{\partial x'^\mu}{\partial x^\lambda}\frac{\partial x^\sigma}{\partial x'^\nu}\, V^\lambda{}_{;\sigma}\): the covariant derivative of a tensor is a tensor with one more lower index.






ImportantProposition 7.5 (Properties of the covariant derivative). [1, Ch. 4]




It is linear and obeys the Leibniz rule.
It commutes with contraction: for instance \(T^{\mu\lambda}{}_{\lambda;\rho} = \partial_\rho T^{\mu\lambda}{}_\lambda + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\eta}\, T^{\eta\lambda}{}_\lambda\), as for a vector.
On scalars it is the partial derivative, \(S_{;\rho} = \partial_\rho S\).
The metric is covariantly constant, \(g_{\mu\nu;\rho} = 0\). Hence raising and lowering indices commutes with covariant differentiation, for example \((g^{\mu\nu} V_\nu)_{;\rho} = g^{\mu\nu}\, V_{\nu;\rho}\).







NoteProof





Items 1–3 follow from the definition. For item 4, \(g_{\mu\nu;\rho} = \partial_\rho g_{\mu\nu} - \Gamma^\sigma_{\mu\rho}\, g_{\sigma\nu} - \Gamma^\sigma_{\nu\rho}\, g_{\mu\sigma}\) is a tensor, and it vanishes in locally inertial coordinates at any point, where \(\partial_\rho g_{\mu\nu} = 0\) and \(\Gamma = 0\). A tensor that vanishes in one coordinate system vanishes in all. \(\square\)
crumbs: 7  Derivatives of Tensors

title: 7  Derivatives of Tensors
text:
Curl and divergence
For the covariant curl of a covariant vector the connection terms cancel, since \(\Gamma^\sigma_{\mu\rho}\) is symmetric: \[V_{\mu;\rho} - V_{\rho;\mu} = \frac{\partial V_\mu}{\partial x^\rho} - \frac{\partial V_\rho}{\partial x^\mu}.\]
For the covariant divergence \(V^\mu{}_{;\mu} = \partial_\mu V^\mu + \Gamma^\mu_{\mu\sigma}\, V^\sigma\) we need the contracted connection. By (5) of Lecture 5, \[\Gamma^\mu_{\mu\sigma} = \tfrac12\, g^{\mu\rho}\, \frac{\partial g_{\rho\mu}}{\partial x^\sigma},\] the other two terms cancelling against each other in the contraction with the symmetric \(g^{\mu\rho}\).






ImportantProposition 7.6 (Covariant divergence). [1, Ch. 4]



\[\Gamma^\mu_{\mu\sigma} = \frac{1}{\sqrt g}\frac{\partial\sqrt g}{\partial x^\sigma}, \qquad V^\mu{}_{;\mu} = \frac{1}{\sqrt g}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu}\bigl(\sqrt g\, V^\mu\bigr).\] In particular, if \(V^\mu\) vanishes at infinity, \(\int d^4x\, \sqrt g\, V^\mu{}_{;\mu} = 0\).






NoteProof





By Jacobi’s formula, \(\partial_\sigma \ln\det M = \operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}\partial_\sigma M)\) for any invertible matrix \(M(x)\). With \(M = g_{\mu\nu}\), \[\tfrac12\, g^{\mu\rho}\, \partial_\sigma g_{\rho\mu} = \tfrac12\, \partial_\sigma \ln g = \frac{1}{\sqrt g}\, \partial_\sigma\sqrt g.\] Inserting this in \(V^\mu{}_{;\mu}\) gives the second formula, and the integral vanishes by the divergence theorem. \(\square\)





For a tensor with two upper indices, \[T^{\mu\nu}{}_{;\mu} = \frac{1}{\sqrt g}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu}\bigl(\sqrt g\, T^{\mu\nu}\bigr) + \Gamma^\nu_{\mu\rho}\, T^{\mu\rho}. \tag{2}\] If \(T^{\mu\nu}\) is antisymmetric, such as the field strength \(F^{\mu\nu}\), the last term vanishes, since \(\Gamma^\nu_{\mu\rho}\) is symmetric in \(\mu\rho\).
Similarly, for an antisymmetric tensor \(A_{\mu\nu}\) the connection terms in the cyclic sum cancel in pairs: \[A_{\mu\nu;\lambda} + A_{\lambda\mu;\nu} + A_{\nu\lambda;\mu} = \frac{\partial A_{\mu\nu}}{\partial x^\lambda} + \frac{\partial A_{\lambda\mu}}{\partial x^\nu} + \frac{\partial A_{\nu\lambda}}{\partial x^\mu}.\] Applied to \(F_{\mu\nu}\), the homogeneous Maxwell equation (4) of Lecture 5 is therefore already generally covariant.

text:
NoteDefinition 8.1 (Covariant derivative along a curve). [1, Ch. 4]



The covariant derivatives along \(x^\mu(\tau)\) of a contravariant and a covariant vector are \[\frac{DA^\mu}{D\tau} = \frac{dA^\mu}{d\tau} + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}\, \frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\, A^\sigma, \qquad \frac{DA_\mu}{D\tau} = \frac{dA_\mu}{d\tau} - \Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma}\, \frac{dx^\sigma}{d\tau}\, A_\rho.\]









NoteDefinition 8.2 (Parallel transport). [1, Ch. 4]



A vector \(A^\mu(\tau)\) is parallel transported along \(x^\mu(\tau)\) if \[\frac{DA^\mu}{D\tau} = \frac{dA^\mu}{d\tau} + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}\, \frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\, A^\sigma = 0.\]

title: 8  The Principle of General Covariance
text:
The principle of general covariance
The principle of general covariance is a mathematical way of stating the equivalence principle.






NoteDefinition 8.3 (Principle of general covariance). [1, Ch. 4]



An equation holds in an arbitrary gravitational field if

it holds in the absence of gravity, that is, it agrees with special relativity when \(g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\mu\nu}\) and \(\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} = 0\); and
it is generally covariant.



The second condition alone is not enough: an equation can be generally covariant and equally wrong in every coordinate system. The first condition ties it to known physics. Together they imply that the equation holds in a general gravitational field. By the equivalence principle there is a locally inertial coordinate system at each point, in which the equation holds by condition 1; by condition 2 it then holds in every coordinate system.






TipRemark 8.4 (Passive and active covariance).



The covariance here is passive: it concerns the form of equations under changes of coordinates. The active version, in which diffeomorphisms move the fields themselves around on a fixed manifold, is the subject of the hole argument.


In practice, a law of special relativity is carried over to general relativity in three steps:

write the equation in a locally inertial coordinate system, as predicted by special relativity;
replace all Lorentz tensors by general tensors;
replace partial derivatives (and \(d/d\tau\)) by covariant derivatives (and \(D/D\tau\)).

The result is generally covariant and reduces to the original equation in the absence of gravity. The procedure is not unique, however: one could add terms involving the curvature (Lecture 9), which vanish when \(g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\mu\nu}\). Step 2 works because contracting Lorentz indices with \(\partial\xi^\alpha/\partial x^\mu\) produces general tensors. For example, \[g_{\mu\nu} = \frac{\partial\xi^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu}\frac{\partial\xi^\beta}{\partial x^\nu}\, \eta_{\alpha\beta}, \qquad T^\mu{}_\nu = \frac{\partial x^\mu}{\partial\xi^\alpha}\frac{\partial\xi^\beta}{\partial x^\nu}\, T^\alpha{}_\beta\] transform as tensors under general coordinate transformations, since the Lorentz indices are summed over.

title: 8  The Principle of General Covariance
text:
Particle mechanics

A freely falling particle
In a locally inertial coordinate system, a freely falling particle with four-velocity \(U^\alpha = d\xi^\alpha/d\tau\) and spin \(S_\alpha\) (Definition 4.9) moves on a straight line, and its spin does not precess: \[\frac{dU^\alpha}{d\tau} = 0, \qquad \frac{dS_\alpha}{d\tau} = 0.\] The vectors \(U^\mu = \frac{\partial x^\mu}{\partial\xi^\alpha}\, U^\alpha\) and \(S_\mu = \frac{\partial\xi^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu}\, S_\alpha\) are general vectors, and step 3 gives \[\frac{DU^\mu}{D\tau} = \frac{dU^\mu}{d\tau} + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}\, \frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\, U^\sigma = 0, \qquad \frac{DS_\mu}{D\tau} = \frac{dS_\mu}{d\tau} - \Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma}\, \frac{dx^\sigma}{d\tau}\, S_\rho = 0.\] The first is the geodesic equation; the second says that the spin is parallel transported. These are the unique answers if we only allow the connection, that is, first derivatives of the metric. Terms with second derivatives of the metric could be added without spoiling either condition of Definition 8.3.


A particle acted on by a force
If a four-force \(f^\alpha\) acts on the particle, special relativity gives \(dU^\alpha/d\tau = f^\alpha/m\) in locally inertial coordinates. With \(f^\mu = \frac{\partial x^\mu}{\partial\xi^\alpha}\, f^\alpha\), \[\frac{DU^\mu}{D\tau} = \frac{f^\mu}{m} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m\, \frac{dU^\mu}{d\tau} = f^\mu - \underbrace{m\, \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}\, \frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\sigma}{d\tau}}_{\text{gravitational force}}.\]


Spin under a force without torque
If the force exerts no torque, the angular momentum is conserved in the rest frame, and in a comoving inertial frame, where \(U^\alpha = (1, 0, 0, 0)\) and \(d\tau = dt\), the spatial components of the spin are constant: \(dS^i/d\tau = 0\). Hence \[\frac{dS^\alpha}{d\tau} = \Phi\, U^\alpha\] for some scalar \(\Phi\). Differentiating \(S_\alpha U^\alpha = 0\) (Proposition 4.10) and using \(U_\alpha U^\alpha = -1\) gives \(\Phi = S_\beta\, dU^\beta/d\tau\), so \[\frac{dS^\alpha}{d\tau} = U^\alpha\, S_\beta\, \frac{dU^\beta}{d\tau}, \tag{1}\] which is Lorentz covariant and so holds in every inertial frame. Equation (1) describes Thomas precession.






TipRemark 8.5 (Thomas precession).



Thomas precession is a kinematic effect, a special case of Wigner rotation: two successive boosts in different directions compose to a boost followed by a rotation. For an electron in an atom it halves the naive spin–orbit coupling, which would otherwise be overestimated by a factor of two.








ImportantProposition 8.6 (Fermi transport). [1, Ch. 5]



In a gravitational field, the spin of a particle acted on by a force without torque obeys \[\frac{DS^\mu}{D\tau} = U^\mu\, S_\nu\, \frac{DU^\nu}{D\tau}.\] When \(f^\mu = 0\), so that \(DU^\nu/D\tau = 0\), this reduces to parallel transport.


This follows from (1) by the three steps above, and is called Fermi transport.

Symmetries






ImportantProposition 9.2 (Symmetries of the Riemann tensor). [1, Ch. 6]



\[\begin{aligned}
R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} &= R_{\rho\sigma\mu\nu}, \\
R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} &= -R_{\nu\mu\rho\sigma} = -R_{\mu\nu\sigma\rho}, \\
0 &= R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} + R_{\mu\sigma\nu\rho} + R_{\mu\rho\sigma\nu}.
\end{aligned}\] Consequently, the Ricci tensor is symmetric, \(R_{\nu\sigma} = R_{\sigma\nu}\).






NoteProof





All four identities are tensor equations, so it suffices to check them in locally inertial coordinates at a point, where \(\Gamma = 0\) and only the second-derivative terms in (2) survive. There they can be read off directly: exchanging \((\mu\nu) \leftrightarrow (\rho\sigma)\) permutes the four terms, exchanging \(\mu \leftrightarrow \nu\) or \(\rho \leftrightarrow \sigma\) flips the sign of each, and in the cyclic sum each second derivative appears twice with opposite signs. For the Ricci tensor, \[R_{\nu\sigma} = g^{\mu\rho} R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = g^{\mu\rho} R_{\rho\sigma\mu\nu} = R_{\sigma\nu}. \qquad \square\]





The Ricci tensor is, up to sign, the only rank-2 tensor that can be built by contracting the Riemann tensor with the metric, and \(R\) is the only such scalar: by the antisymmetries every other contraction vanishes or gives \(\pm R_{\mu\nu}\).






ImportantProposition 9.3 (Number of independent components). [1, Ch. 6]



In \(N\) dimensions the Riemann tensor has \(N^2(N^2 - 1)/12\) independent components; in four dimensions, 20.






NoteProof





By the antisymmetries, think of \(R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\) as a matrix \(R_{(\mu\nu)(\rho\sigma)}\) indexed by antisymmetric pairs. Each pair takes \(M = N(N-1)/2\) values, and by the pair symmetry the matrix is symmetric, which leaves \[\tfrac12 M(M + 1) = \tfrac18 N(N-1)(N^2 - N + 2)\] components. Given the other symmetries, the cyclic identity is a non-trivial condition only when all four indices are distinct, which gives \(\binom N4 = N(N-1)(N-2)(N-3)/24\) further constraints. Subtracting, \[\tfrac18 N(N-1)(N^2 - N + 2) - \tfrac1{24} N(N-1)(N-2)(N-3) = \tfrac1{12} N^2(N^2 - 1). \qquad \square\]

title: 10  The Bianchi Identities and Geodesic Deviation
text:
ImportantProposition 10.1 (Bianchi identities). [1, Ch. 6]



The Riemann tensor satisfies \[R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma;\lambda} + R_{\mu\nu\lambda\rho;\sigma} + R_{\mu\nu\sigma\lambda;\rho} = 0. \tag{1}\]






NoteProof





This is a tensor equation, so we check it in locally inertial coordinates at a point. There \(\Gamma = 0\), so covariant derivatives are partial derivatives, and the \(\Gamma\Gamma\) terms in (2) of Lecture 9 have vanishing first derivatives. Hence \[R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma;\lambda} = \tfrac12\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^\lambda}\Bigl(\frac{\partial^2 g_{\mu\rho}}{\partial x^\sigma \partial x^\nu} - \frac{\partial^2 g_{\nu\rho}}{\partial x^\sigma \partial x^\mu} - \frac{\partial^2 g_{\mu\sigma}}{\partial x^\rho \partial x^\nu} + \frac{\partial^2 g_{\nu\sigma}}{\partial x^\rho \partial x^\mu}\Bigr),\] and in the cyclic sum over \((\rho, \sigma, \lambda)\) every third derivative appears twice with opposite signs. \(\square\)











ImportantProposition 10.2 (Contracted Bianchi identities). [1, Ch. 6]



\[\Bigl(R^{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12\, g^{\mu\nu} R\Bigr)_{;\mu} = 0.\]






NoteProof





Contract \(\mu\) with \(\rho\) in (1). Since the metric is covariantly constant (Proposition 7.5), contraction commutes with differentiation, and using the antisymmetry in the last pair, \[R_{\nu\sigma;\lambda} - R_{\nu\lambda;\sigma} + R^\rho{}_{\nu\sigma\lambda;\rho} = 0.\] Contracting \(\nu\) with \(\sigma\) gives \[R_{;\lambda} - R^\sigma{}_{\lambda;\sigma} - R^\rho{}_{\lambda;\rho} = 0, \quad\text{that is}\quad \bigl(R^\sigma{}_\lambda - \tfrac12\, \delta^\sigma_\lambda R\bigr)_{;\sigma} = 0.\] Raising \(\lambda\) gives the result. \(\square\)

title: 10  The Bianchi Identities and Geodesic Deviation
text:
Geodesic deviation
Consider two freely falling particles. If they are close enough, a freely falling observer can describe both with a single locally inertial coordinate system, and sees no effect of gravity: the particles stay at rest relative to each other. If they are far enough apart to resolve, say, the curvature of the Earth, no single locally inertial system covers both, and the observer sees them accelerate towards each other (Figure 10.1). The relative motion of nearby free particles is what reveals gravity.






Figure 10.1: Two particles dropped side by side above the Earth fall along radial lines towards its centre, so their separation shrinks as they fall. A freely falling observer between them sees them accelerate towards each other: a tidal effect that cannot be transformed away.



Let particle 1 follow \(x^\mu(\tau)\) and particle 2 follow \(x^\mu(\tau) + \delta x^\mu(\tau)\), both geodesics: \[\frac{d^2x^\mu}{d\tau^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}(x)\, \frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\sigma}{d\tau} = 0, \qquad \frac{d^2(x^\mu + \delta x^\mu)}{d\tau^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}(x + \delta x)\, \frac{d(x^\rho + \delta x^\rho)}{d\tau}\frac{d(x^\sigma + \delta x^\sigma)}{d\tau} = 0.\] Subtracting, to first order in \(\delta x\), \[\frac{d^2\delta x^\mu}{d\tau^2} + \frac{\partial\Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}}{\partial x^\lambda}\frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\sigma}{d\tau}\, \delta x^\lambda + 2\Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}\, \frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\frac{d\delta x^\sigma}{d\tau} = 0. \tag{2}\]






ImportantProposition 10.3 (Geodesic deviation). [1, Ch. 6]



The separation \(\delta x^\mu\) of two neighbouring geodesics satisfies \[\frac{D^2\delta x^\mu}{D\tau^2} + R^\mu{}_{\rho\sigma\lambda}\, \frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\sigma}{d\tau}\, \delta x^\lambda = 0.\]






NoteProof





By Definition 8.1, \[\frac{D\delta x^\mu}{D\tau} = \frac{d\delta x^\mu}{d\tau} + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}\, \frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\, \delta x^\sigma,\] and applying \(D/D\tau\) once more, \[\frac{D^2\delta x^\mu}{D\tau^2} = \frac{d^2\delta x^\mu}{d\tau^2} + \frac{\partial\Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}}{\partial x^\lambda}\frac{dx^\lambda}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\, \delta x^\sigma + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}\, \frac{d^2x^\rho}{d\tau^2}\, \delta x^\sigma + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\sigma}\, \frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\frac{d\delta x^\sigma}{d\tau} + \Gamma^\mu_{\eta\xi}\, \frac{dx^\eta}{d\tau}\frac{D\delta x^\xi}{D\tau}.\] Eliminate \(d^2\delta x^\mu/d\tau^2\) with (2) and \(d^2x^\rho/d\tau^2\) with the geodesic equation. The terms in \(d\delta x/d\tau\) cancel, and the remaining terms, all proportional to \(\delta x^\lambda\, \frac{dx^\rho}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\sigma}{d\tau}\), combine into \(-R^\mu{}_{\rho\sigma\lambda}\) by Definition 9.1. \(\square\)





If the Riemann tensor vanishes, nearby free particles do not accelerate relative to each other, and there is no gravitational field in any physical sense. The converse is also true.






ImportantTheorem 10.4 (Flat metrics). [1, Ch. 6]



There is a coordinate transformation \(x \mapsto \xi(x)\) such that \[\eta^{\alpha\beta} = \frac{\partial\xi^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu}\frac{\partial\xi^\beta}{\partial x^\nu}\, g^{\mu\nu}\] everywhere if and only if

\(R^\mu{}_{\nu\rho\sigma} = 0\) everywhere, and
at some point, \(g_{\mu\nu}\) has the same number of positive and negative eigenvalues as \(\eta_{\mu\nu}\).



The theorem decides whether a given metric is Minkowski space written in curvilinear coordinates, or a genuinely different geometry.

title: 10  The Bianchi Identities and Geodesic Deviation
text:
Curvature and non-Euclidean geometry






NoteDefinition 10.5 (Euclidean geometry).



Euclidean plane geometry rests on five postulates:

any two points can be joined by a straight line segment;
any line segment can be extended indefinitely;
a circle can be drawn with any centre and any radius;
all right angles are congruent;
through a point not on a given line there is exactly one line that does not meet the given line (the parallel postulate).

A geometry is non-Euclidean if it satisfies the first four postulates but not the fifth.


The two-sphere is an example, with great circles as its straight lines (they are the shortest paths between points). Any two great circles meet: two lines that are both perpendicular to the equator, and so “parallel” there, meet at the poles.






NoteDefinition 10.6 (Geodesic curve, affine parameter). [1, Ch. 6]



A curve is a geodesic if it admits a parametrisation whose tangent vector is parallel transported along it, \[\frac{d^2x^i}{d\lambda^2} + \Gamma^i_{lm}\, \frac{dx^l}{d\lambda}\frac{dx^m}{d\lambda} = 0.\] Such a parameter \(\lambda\) is called affine.


A geodesic is thus a curve that parallel transports its own tangent vector. More generally, a curve whose tangent \(W\) satisfies \(\nabla_W W \propto W\) can always be reparametrised so that \(\nabla_W W = 0\).






CautionExample 10.7 (The plane).



In Cartesian coordinates the plane has \(g_{ij} = \delta_{ij}\), so \(\Gamma^l_{ij} = 0\), and parallel transport is \(dV_i/d\lambda = 0\): vectors are constant. In particular, a vector carried around any closed curve returns to itself. For a small closed curve in a general space, the change is \[\Delta V_i = \tfrac12\, R^l{}_{ijm}\, V_l \oint \xi^m\, d\xi^j,\] so in the plane \(R^l{}_{ijm} = 0\).








CautionExample 10.8 (The sphere).



On a sphere of radius \(a\) in coordinates \((\theta, \phi)\), \[ds^2 = a^2\bigl(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\, d\phi^2\bigr),\] with non-zero connection coefficients \(\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi} = -\sin\theta\cos\theta\) and \(\Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi} = \Gamma^\phi_{\phi\theta} = \cot\theta\). These depend on \(\theta\), and parallel transport is non-trivial.
On the equator \(\theta = \pi/2\) all of them vanish, so a vector carried along the equator keeps its components. Carry a vector from the north pole down a meridian, a quarter of the way along the equator and back up another meridian (Figure 10.2). Each leg is a geodesic, along which the angle between the vector and the tangent stays fixed, and the vector returns to the pole rotated by \(\pi/2\), the angle enclosed at the pole. The curvature of the sphere is seen in this failure of a vector to return to itself.








Figure 10.2: Parallel transport around a geodesic triangle with three right angles. The vector returns to the north pole rotated by \(\pi/2\), the angle the triangle encloses at the pole.



Non-vanishing curvature \(R^\mu{}_{\nu\rho\sigma} \neq 0\) thus signals both that the geometry is non-Euclidean and, by geodesic deviation, that gravity is present. This is the link between gravity and geometry on which general relativity rests.

title: 11  The Einstein Equations
text:
The cosmological constant
Terms with one derivative cannot contribute, since they vanish in locally inertial coordinates. But a term with \(N = 0\) derivatives is allowed: the metric itself.






NoteDefinition 11.3 (Cosmological constant). [1, Ch. 7]



With a cosmological constant \(\lambda\), the Einstein equations read \[R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12\, g_{\mu\nu} R - \lambda\, g_{\mu\nu} = -8\pi G\, T_{\mu\nu}.\]


The new term is still conserved, since \(g_{\mu\nu;\lambda} = 0\). Einstein introduced it to allow a static, non-expanding universe. When the expansion of the Universe was discovered the term was dropped, but the later discovery that the expansion is accelerating brought it back (Lecture 21). It must be small, so as not to conflict with Newtonian gravity on the scale of the solar system.

title: 12  The Cauchy Problem and Harmonic Coordinates
text:
The Cauchy problem
Suppose \(g_{\mu
u}\) and \(\partial_0 g_{\mu
u}\) are known on a surface \(x^0 = t\). Can we find \(g_{\mu
u}\) at later times? Stepping forward in time, \[ egin{aligned}
g_{\mu
u}(t + \delta t, x^i) &= g_{\mu
u}(t, x^i) + \partial_0 g_{\mu
u}(t, x^i)\, \delta t, \
\partial_0 g_{\mu
u}(t + \delta t, x^i) &= \partial_0 g_{\mu
u}(t, x^i) + \underbrace{\partial_0^2 g_{\mu
u}(t, x^i)}_{	ext{from the Einstein equations}}\, \delta t,
\end{aligned}\] so we need the Einstein equations to give all ten second time derivatives \(\partial_0^2 g_{\mu
u}\). This is the Cauchy problem.
The six equations \(G^{ij} = -8\pi G\, T^{ij}\) can be solved for the six \(\partial_0^2 g_{ij}\). The remaining four, \(G^{0\mu} = -8\pi G\, T^{0\mu}\), do not determine \(\partial_0^2 g_{0\mu}\).
The four equations \(G^{0\mu} = -8\pi G\, T^{0\mu}\) are therefore not evolution equations but constraints on the initial data. This leaves four functions undetermined, which correspond to the four functions \(x'^\mu(x)\) of a general coordinate transformation: given a solution, any coordinate transformation that is trivial at the initial time gives another solution with the same initial data. To obtain a unique solution, one must fix the coordinate system, that is, break the general covariance of the equations. How best to do so depends on the problem. One convenient choice is the harmonic coordinates.

title: 12  The Cauchy Problem and Harmonic Coordinates

ImportantProposition 12.1 (The \(G^{0\mu}\) equations are constraints). [1, Ch. 7]



\(G^{0\mu}\) contains at most first time derivatives of the metric.






NoteProof





By the contracted Bianchi identities (Proposition 10.2), \[-\frac{\partial G^{0\nu}}{\partial x^0} = \frac{\partial G^{i\nu}}{\partial x^i} + \Gamma^\mu_{\rho\mu}\, G^{\rho\nu} + \Gamma^\nu_{\rho\mu}\, G^{\mu\rho}.\] The right-hand side contains at most second time derivatives, since \(G^{\mu\nu}\) does. If \(G^{0\nu}\) contained a second time derivative, the left-hand side would contain a third. \(\square\)
